howVerify.afterATablePassesWeTakeAFingerprint: After a table passes, we take a fingerprint of it and store that fingerprint in the repository. From then on, if a single digit in that table changes, the verification suite stops before the browser checks and reports the mismatch. Re-verifying the data and deliberately updating the fingerprint are separate human steps, not something the seal can enforce by itself.
howVerify.backTranslationCatchesMissingWarnings: Back-translation catches missing warnings and mangled meaning. It is a screen, not proof.
howVerify.beClearAboutWhatThisDoesAndDoesnTProve: The seal proves a number hasn't changed without somebody noticing. It doesn't prove the original was right. That's what the multi-source check is for. They're separate protections and they do separate jobs.
howVerify.codesAreAdoptedLocally: Codes are adopted locally and amended locally. The edition in force where you're standing may not be the one a table came from.
howVerify.everyCalculatorIsDrivenInAllSixEditions: Every calculator is driven in all six editions, not just English, and the answer is checked against an expected value — hand-worked for the core voltage-drop cases, and derived from the sealed tables for the rest. We learned this one the hard way: a test run that drove only English once reported a clean pass while the main calculator was dead in four other editions.
howVerify.everyNumberShownOnATranslatedPage: The numeric-parity check covers the translated guides, the Terms page, and three newer pages, including this one. On those pages, every visible number is compared with its English twin, except for a value explicitly marked as a legitimate locale-specific difference.
howVerify.ifANumberHereLooksWrong: If a number here looks wrong to you, say so. You don't need to be polite about it. Corrections to safety data get priority over everything else on the roadmap.
howVerify.ifAPageHereShowsYouAResult: So read the labels rather than assuming. Where the data behind a result hasn't passed for your country, the page tells you so in plain language instead of quietly presenting it as a verified answer.
howVerify.noLicensedElectricianReviewsOrApproves: No licensed electrician reviews or approves VoltDrop. Nobody here is holding a licence over this work. If a page ever claims otherwise, it's wrong — tell us.
howVerify.ourCanadianConduitFillPageCarriesAPlanni: The Canadian conduit-fill page shows what happens when a gap closes. It used to carry a warning because its Canadian conductor and conduit tables had not passed the multi-source check. CSA C22.1:24 Tables 6A/6K and 9A–9H have now passed, so the warning is gone and the page computes from sealed Canadian data. We would rather leave a visible gap than fill it early, and remove the warning only when the evidence changes.
howVerify.readHowVoltDropChecksItsNumbers: Read how VoltDrop checks its numbers
howVerify.resultsArePlanningEstimates: Results are planning estimates using simplified, normal-conditions methods. Real installations have conditions our inputs don't ask about.
howVerify.termsThatMustNeverBeTranslated: Terms that must never be translated — code names, wire types, and units — are checked for survival in every language.
howVerify.theEasiestThingWouldBeToFillEveryGap: The easiest thing in the world would be to fill every gap with a plausible-looking number and say nothing about it. When a country-specific table has not passed, we label the boundary or refuse the answer in the place you would be about to rely on it.
howVerify.theEnglishPagesAreComparedByteForByte: The English pages are compared byte-for-byte against the previous build, so nothing changes by accident.
howVerify.thisIsNotTheatreOneDraftAmpacity: This is not theatre. One draft ampacity value in an early build disagreed between sources. The check caught it, the value was corrected before it shipped, and that is the whole reason the step exists.
howVerify.voltDropDoesnTTypeNumbersInFromMemory: VoltDrop doesn't type numbers in from memory. Every electrical table built into these calculators is compared against at least two independently produced reproductions of the published table before it goes live, row by row. They all have to agree, on every cell, or it doesn't ship.
howVerify.voltDropShipsInSixEditionsAcrossFourLang: VoltDrop ships in six editions across four languages. A safety warning that quietly loses its meaning in translation is a real hazard, so we screen for it: the translated text is turned back into English on its own, without the original in view, and the result is compared against what we actually meant.

howVerify.weAlsoWatchTheScreenItself: We also watch the screen itself. An early version of this check reported almost everything as perfect because the English original had leaked into the process and was simply being echoed back. That run was thrown out. The check was rebuilt so the source is sealed out of it. Runs that show signs of leakage are rejected rather than trusted.

fiftyAmp.n6CopperForRomexNMBCableAnswer: #6 copper for Romex/NM-B cable, #8 copper THHN in conduit with 75°C terminations, or #6 aluminum — for a 240 V circuit at ordinary distances. Over about 100 feet, upsize for voltage drop.
fiftyAmp.n6CopperIfYouReUsingRomex: #6 copper if you're using Romex/NM-B cable
fiftyAmp.n6CopperIsTheStandardAnswerRunAnswer: #6 copper is the standard answer, run as a 4-wire circuit with GFCI protection and a disconnect within sight of the tub. Long runs from the panel should be checked for voltage drop.
fiftyAmp.n6CopperOrN4AluminumKeepsVoltageAnswer: #6 copper or #4 aluminum keeps voltage drop under the 3% planning target at 240 V and 50 A over 100 one-way feet.

fiftyAmp.sameSizingButIfThePedestalIs: same sizing, but if the pedestal is far from the panel, use the distance table — RV pads at 150+ feet routinely need #4.

The code assigns every wire an amp rating by its insulation temperature column. #8 copper is rated exactly 50 A in the 75°C column — fine for THHN in conduit landing on standard 75°C-rated breaker lugs. But Romex (NM-B cable) must use the 60°C column no matter what's printed on the conductors, and #8 NM-B is only good for 40 A — so Romex needs #6. Sites that say "always #6" are being safe; sites that say "#8" are assuming conduit. Both are quoting real rows of the same table — check it yourself in the

fiftyAmp.theTwoMostCommonAnswersOnlineAre: The two most common answers online are "#6" and "#8," and the argument is really about
fiftyAmp.usuallyAN4WireCircuitTwoHots: usually a 4-wire circuit (two hots, neutral, ground) with a GFCI breaker or GFCI spa disconnect within sight of the tub — #6 copper NM-B indoors transitioning to THHN in conduit outdoors is the classic setup.
fiftyAmp.weldersGetSpecialTreatmentTheirDutyCycle: welders get special treatment (their duty cycle legally allows smaller wire than the breaker suggests — genuinely counterintuitive), so don't panic if a welder manual specifies less.
fiftyAmp.whatSizeWireDoINeedForQuestion: What size wire do I need for a 50 amp breaker?
fiftyAmp.whatSizeWireForAN50AmpQuestion: What size wire for a 50 amp hot tub?
fiftyAmp.whatSizeWireForN50AmpsAtQuestion: What size wire for 50 amps at 100 feet?
fiftyAmp.workedExampleN50AHotTubAtHeading: Worked example: 50 A hot tub at 80 feet
fiftyAmp.yesIfItSAnIndividualConductorAnswer: Yes, if it's an individual conductor type like THHN in conduit with 75°C-rated terminations — #8 copper is rated exactly 50 A in the NEC 75°C column. No, if it's NM-B (Romex), which is limited to the 60°C column where #8 is only 40 A.

twentyAmp.aluminumBranchWireIsNotShownNote: Small-gauge aluminum branch-circuit wire is not shown. Use copper here; check any other wiring method in the Ampacity Check tool.
twentyAmp.canIUseN14GaugeOnAN20AmpBreakerQuestion: Can I use 14 gauge wire on a 20 amp breaker?
twentyAmp.forOrdinaryN20AmpBranchCircuitsAnswer: Use 12 AWG copper for an ordinary 20 A branch circuit. NEC 240.4(D) caps 14 AWG copper at 15 A, so it cannot be protected by a 20 A breaker for this ordinary use.
twentyAmp.howFarCanIRunN12GaugeOnN20AmpsQuestion: How far can I run 12 gauge wire on 20 amps?
twentyAmp.howFarN12GaugeGuide: How far can you run 12 gauge wire?
twentyAmp.jobsBody: Kitchen small-appliance circuits, bathrooms, garage receptacles, and general lighting are common 20 A jobs. The appliance instructions and local rules still control the final design.
twentyAmp.minimumCopperSizeAtN120VBody: Minimum copper size at 120 V, sized at the full 20 A and kept at or under the 3% voltage-drop target (one-way distance):
twentyAmp.nECN240N4DCapsN14AWG: NEC 240.4(D) caps 14 AWG copper at 15 A and 12 AWG copper at 20 A for ordinary circuits. A larger raw ampacity in another temperature column does not erase that cap.
twentyAmp.theEverydayAnswerIsN12AWG: The everyday answer is 12 AWG copper. Do not put 14 AWG copper on a 20 A breaker for an ordinary branch circuit.
twentyAmp.whatSizeWireForN20AmpCircuitTitle: 🔌 What Size Wire for a 20 Amp Circuit?
twentyAmp.workedExampleHeading: Worked example: 20 A at 120 V over 100 feet
twentyAmp.workedExampleBody: Our verified calculator selects #8 copper (16,510 circular mils): 2 × 12.9 × 20 × 100 ÷ 16,510 = 3.13 V, or 2.6% of 120 V. It passes both the ampacity check and the 3% drop target.
twentyAmp.yesN12AWGIsTheStartingAnswerAnswer: 12 AWG is the starting answer, but its useful distance depends on voltage and load. Use the dedicated distance guide or enter the exact run in the Wire Size calculator.
twentyAmp.atN240VTheAmpacityFloorStaysAnswer: The ampacity floor stays 12 AWG copper at 20 A, but 240 V gives more voltage-drop room than 120 V. Enter the actual distance and voltage in the Wire Size calculator.

thirtyAmp.aluminumDecisionBody: The verified ampacity table supports #8 aluminum at 30 A under ordinary 75°C termination conditions, so aluminum is included. Confirm the conductor type, terminals, and equipment listing before using it.
thirtyAmp.dryerWireSizeQuestion: What size wire does a 30 amp dryer use?
thirtyAmp.jobsBody: Dryers, water heaters, RV receptacles, and some mini-split or air-conditioning circuits commonly land near this rating. Use the equipment nameplate when it gives a different circuit requirement.
thirtyAmp.minimumSizeBody: Minimum size at the full 30 A and at or under 3% voltage drop. Distance is one way; the calculator also rejects any size that fails ampacity.
thirtyAmp.tableN240VHeading: 30 A at 240 V — dryer or water heater
thirtyAmp.theStartingAnswerIsN10AWG: Start with 10 AWG copper for an ordinary 30 A circuit. A TT-30 RV receptacle is 120 V, while a typical dryer or water-heater circuit is 240 V; that voltage difference changes long-run sizing.
thirtyAmp.whatSizeWireForAN30AmpDryerAnswer: Start with 10 AWG copper for an ordinary 30 A dryer circuit. Check the appliance instructions, cable type, and distance before installation.
thirtyAmp.whatSizeWireForAN30AmpRVPlugQuestion: What size wire for a 30 amp RV plug?
thirtyAmp.whatSizeWireForN30AmpBreakerTitle: 🔌 What Size Wire for a 30 Amp Breaker?
thirtyAmp.workedExampleHeading: Worked example: 30 A RV receptacle at 100 feet
thirtyAmp.workedExampleBody: At 120 V, our verified calculator selects #6 copper (26,240 circular mils): 2 × 12.9 × 30 × 100 ÷ 26,240 = 2.95 V, or 2.46%. The 240 V table is smaller because the same volts lost are half the percentage.
thirtyAmp.noN12AWGCopperIsCappedAnswer: No. NEC 240.4(D) caps 12 AWG copper at 20 A for ordinary circuits, so it does not pass a 30 A ampacity check.
thirtyAmp.aTTN30IsAN120VAnswer: A TT-30 RV receptacle is 120 V. Start with 10 AWG copper at ordinary distances, then use the 120 V table or calculator for the actual one-way run.

fortyAmp.canIRunAnEVChargerOnAN40AmpCircuitQuesti: Can I run an EV charger on a 40 amp circuit?
fortyAmp.diagramN8CopperAtN60AndN75AriaLabel: Diagram: 8 AWG copper is rated 40 amps at 60 degrees C and 50 amps at 75 degrees C under ordinary conditions
fortyAmp.isN8GaugeEnoughForN40AmpsQuestion: Is 8 gauge wire enough for 40 amps?
fortyAmp.jobsBody: A range is the classic 40 A circuit. A 32 A continuous EV load also lands on a 40 A circuit because 32 A × 1.25 = 40 A; confirm the charger's setting and installation instructions.
fortyAmp.minimumSizeAtN240VBody: Minimum size at 240 V, sized at the full 40 A and kept at or under 3% voltage drop (one-way distance):
fortyAmp.rangeWireSizeQuestion: What size wire for a 40 amp range?
fortyAmp.theAnswerIsN8AWGCopper: Use 8 AWG copper for an ordinary 40 A circuit. Unlike the smaller branch-circuit sizes, the answer now depends directly on the allowed temperature column and the wiring method.
fortyAmp.temperatureColumnBody: The verified ampacity table gives #8 copper 40 A in the 60°C column and 50 A in the 75°C column. That makes #8 the minimum at ordinary conditions in either case, but the available headroom is different.
fortyAmp.whatSizeWireForN40AmpBreakerTitle: 🔌 What Size Wire for a 40 Amp Breaker?
fortyAmp.workedExampleHeading: Worked example: 40 A at 240 V over 150 feet
fortyAmp.workedExampleBody: Our verified calculator selects #6 copper (26,240 circular mils): 2 × 12.9 × 40 × 150 ÷ 26,240 = 5.90 V, or 2.46% of 240 V. #8 passes ampacity but does not meet the 3% drop target at this distance.
fortyAmp.yesAtOrdinaryConditionsAnswer: Yes, under ordinary conditions when the wiring method and termination rating support the applicable ampacity column. Heat, bundled conductors, and long distance can require a larger conductor.
fortyAmp.startWithN8CopperForARangeAnswer: Start with 8 AWG copper for an ordinary 40 A range circuit, then follow the appliance instructions and check voltage drop for a long run.
fortyAmp.aN32AContinuousChargerMathAnswer: A 32 A continuous charger produces a 40 A sizing load: 32 A × 1.25 = 40 A. The charger must be set and listed for that circuit, and the conductor still has to pass the installation's ampacity and distance checks.

sixtyAmp.canIRunAnEVChargerOnAN60AmpCircuitQuesti: Can I run an EV charger on a 60 amp circuit?
sixtyAmp.diagramN6VsN4CopperAriaLabel: Diagram: 6 AWG copper reaches 65 amps at 75 degrees C, while the 60 degree C lookup requires 4 AWG copper at 70 amps
sixtyAmp.jobsBody: A 48 A continuous EV charger produces a 60 A sizing load: 48 A × 1.25 = 60 A. Other common jobs include sub-panel feeds and larger heat-pump or mini-split circuits; follow the equipment nameplate.
sixtyAmp.minimumSizeAtN240VBody: Minimum size at 240 V, sized at the full 60 A and kept at or under 3% voltage drop (one-way distance):
sixtyAmp.theAnswerSplitsAtTheTemperatureColumn: The copper answer splits by temperature column: #6 at 75°C, but #4 at 60°C. Check the cable type and terminal markings before choosing between them.
sixtyAmp.theN75CTableGivesN6CopperBody: The verified 75°C column gives #6 copper 65 A, so it passes 60 A. The verified 60°C column gives #6 copper only 55 A, so that method selects #4 copper at 70 A. This page does not use a next-size-up exception to make #6 pass at 60°C.
sixtyAmp.whatSizeWireForN60AmpBreakerTitle: 🔌 What Size Wire for a 60 Amp Breaker?
sixtyAmp.whyDoPeopleSayN6AndN4ForQuestion: Why do people say both 6 and 4 gauge for 60 amps?
sixtyAmp.workedExampleHeading: Worked example: 60 A at 240 V over 150 feet
sixtyAmp.workedExampleBody: Our verified calculator selects #4 copper (41,740 circular mils): 2 × 12.9 × 60 × 150 ÷ 41,740 = 5.56 V, or 2.32% of 240 V. Distance now governs over the #6 copper 75°C ampacity floor.
sixtyAmp.aN48AContinuousChargerMathAnswer: A 48 A continuous charger produces a 60 A sizing load: 48 A × 1.25 = 60 A. Confirm the charger's permitted setting, wiring method, terminal ratings, and local requirements.
sixtyAmp.itDependsOnTheTemperatureColumnAnswer: Because both are real table answers. #6 copper passes in the 75°C column at 65 A; the 60°C lookup requires #4 copper because #6 is only 55 A there.
sixtyAmp.useTheSubPanelGuideAnswer: Use the sub-panel guide for feeder details and distance tables. This page only answers the 60 A breaker-and-conductor view.

hundredAmpService.aluminumBody: Aluminum is common at service sizes because it reduces conductor weight and material cost. Use conductors, terminals, and equipment listed for the material, and have the complete service design checked locally.
hundredAmpService.doesTheN83%RuleApplyToRomexQuestion: Does the 83% rule apply to Romex?
hundredAmpService.distanceBody: This table starts with the NEC 310.12 dwelling-service minimum, then raises the conductor when needed to keep calculated drop at or under the 3% planning target. It uses 240 V, the full 100 A rating, and one-way distance.
hundredAmpService.distanceHeading: Long service laterals and voltage drop
hundredAmpService.dwellingArithmeticBody: 100 A × 83% = 83 A → 4 AWG copper (85 A at 75 °C); 2 AWG aluminum (90 A at 75 °C).
hundredAmpService.feederForkBody: A feeder carrying the entire dwelling load may use the same allowance when every condition below is met. Feeding a 100 A sub-panel that does not carry the whole dwelling is a different job; its ordinary feeder sizing and distance tables are covered here:
hundredAmpService.n100AmpSubPanelWireQuestion: What wire size should I use for a 100 amp sub-panel?
hundredAmpService.noDeratingCondition: No ampacity adjustment or correction factors can be required.
hundredAmpService.notForRomexAnswer: No. NM/Romex is treated as a 60 °C assembly, while this dwelling-service allowance requires conductors rated 75 °C or better.
hundredAmpService.onlyQualifyingDwellingAnswer: Yes for a qualifying 100 A dwelling service: the 83% calculation requires 83 A, and 4 AWG copper is rated 85 A in the verified 75 °C table. Otherwise, check the actual method in the Ampacity Check tool.
hundredAmpService.rangeCondition: The service or feeder rating must be from 100 A through 400 A.
hundredAmpService.serviceConditionsHeading: All four conditions for the 83% allowance
hundredAmpService.shortAnswerBody: A 100 A dwelling service that meets NEC 310.12 can use 4 AWG copper or 2 AWG aluminum. That is a service answer, not a general 100 A feeder answer.
hundredAmpService.standardArithmeticBody: Plain 75 °C table: 100 A → 3 AWG copper (100 A) or 1 AWG aluminum (100 A).
hundredAmpService.standardSizingBody: Without the dwelling-service allowance, use the ordinary ampacity table and the temperature method the installation permits. This includes non-dwelling work and any installation where derating applies. At 75 °C, the verified table selects 3 AWG copper or 1 AWG aluminum. A 60 °C method needs its own lookup and cannot borrow the 75 °C result.
hundredAmpService.subPanelGuideAnswer: Use the 100-amp sub-panel wire size guide. It owns the feeder distance tables and checks that job under the ordinary feeder rules.
hundredAmpService.temperatureMethodCondition: Conductors must be rated 75 °C or better. NM/Romex is a 60 °C assembly, so it is out.
hundredAmpService.theServiceAnswerIsN4Copper: For a qualifying dwelling service, the verified result is 4 AWG copper or 2 AWG aluminum.
hundredAmpService.whatSizeWireForN100AmpServiceTitle: 🏠 What Size Wire for a 100 Amp Service?
hundredAmpService.wholeDwellingCondition: Dwelling service or a feeder carrying the entire dwelling load only — never a branch circuit or a non-dwelling installation.
hundredAmpService.whyChooseCopperOrAluminumQuestion: Should I use copper or aluminum for a 100 amp service?
hundredAmpService.bothMaterialsCanWorkAnswer: Both can work when the equipment and installation are listed for the conductor. The dwelling-service derivation gives 4 AWG copper and 2 AWG aluminum; aluminum is often chosen to reduce weight and material cost.

twoHundredAmpService.aluminumBody: Aluminum is widely used for service conductors because its lower weight and material cost matter at large sizes. Use listed conductors and terminals, follow the equipment instructions, and have the complete service design checked locally.
twoHundredAmpService.aluminumHeading: Why aluminum is common in service work
twoHundredAmpService.canIUseN4N0AluminumForN200AmpServiceQues: Can I use 4/0 aluminum for a 200 amp service?
twoHundredAmpService.distanceBody: This table begins with the NEC 310.12 dwelling-service minimum, then raises the conductor when the calculated drop would exceed the 3% planning target. It uses 240 V, the full 200 A rating, and one-way distance.
twoHundredAmpService.distanceHeading: Distance can move the answer again
twoHundredAmpService.doesRomexQualifyQuestion: Does Romex qualify for the 83% dwelling-service rule?
twoHundredAmpService.dwellingArithmeticBody: 200 A × 83% = 166 A → 2/0 AWG copper (175 A at 75 °C); 4/0 AWG aluminum (180 A at 75 °C).
twoHundredAmpService.n200AmpAluminumServiceWireSizeQuestion: What is the aluminum service wire size for 200 amps?
twoHundredAmpService.noDeratingCondition: No ampacity adjustment or correction factors can be required.
twoHundredAmpService.notForRomexAnswer: No. NM/Romex is a 60 °C assembly, and the dwelling-service allowance requires conductors rated 75 °C or better.
twoHundredAmpService.rangeCondition: The service or feeder rating must be from 100 A through 400 A.
twoHundredAmpService.shortAnswerHeading: Why the internet gives three answers
twoHundredAmpService.standardArithmeticBody: Plain 75 °C table: 200 A → 3/0 AWG copper (200 A) or 250 kcmil aluminum (205 A).
twoHundredAmpService.temperatureMethodCondition: Conductors must be rated 75 °C or better. NM/Romex is a 60 °C assembly, so it is out.
twoHundredAmpService.theThreeAnswersBody: 2/0 AWG copper is the NEC 310.12 dwelling-service answer. 3/0 AWG copper is the plain 310.16 answer at 75 °C when that allowance does not apply. 4/0 AWG aluminum is the dwelling-service aluminum answer; the plain 75 °C table instead selects 250 kcmil aluminum.
twoHundredAmpService.theThreeAnswersSubtitle: 2/0 copper, 3/0 copper, and 4/0 aluminum can all be correct — but under different sizing methods.
twoHundredAmpService.twoN0OrThreeN0ForN200AmpsQuestion: Do I need 2/0 or 3/0 copper for 200 amps?
twoHundredAmpService.twoN0OrThreeN0ForkAnswer: Use 2/0 copper for a dwelling service or whole-dwelling feeder that meets every NEC 310.12 condition. Use 3/0 copper for the plain 75 °C Table 310.16 method when the allowance does not apply.
twoHundredAmpService.useN4N0WhenConditionsPassAnswer: Yes, when the 200 A installation qualifies for NEC 310.12 and the conductors and equipment are suitable for aluminum. The 83% requirement is 166 A, and 4/0 aluminum is rated 180 A at 75 °C.
twoHundredAmpService.whatSizeWireForN200AmpServiceTitle: 🏠 What Size Wire for a 200 Amp Service?
twoHundredAmpService.wholeDwellingCondition: Dwelling service or a feeder carrying the entire dwelling load only — never a branch circuit or a non-dwelling installation.
twoHundredAmpService.n4N0DwellingAnswer: For a qualifying dwelling service, use 4/0 aluminum. Without the allowance, the verified 75 °C table requires 250 kcmil aluminum for 200 A.

necVsCec.ampacityBody: CEC Tables 2 and 4 are numerically identical to NEC 310.16 in the 60/75/90°C columns at every shared size. The old “14 AWG copper is 20 A in Canada” difference was real in the 2012 edition. It was harmonized away around 2015–2018. Anyone repeating it is a decade out of date. But the free-air tables still differ. The harmonization is not total.
necVsCec.colourCanada: Canada, three-phase where colour coding is required: red = A, black = B, blue = C.
necVsCec.colourClose: A and B are effectively swapped across the border.
necVsCec.colourHeading: 7. Conductor colour: the phases are not in the same order
necVsCec.colourUs: The common US convention is black = A, red = B, blue = C. The NEC does not mandate ungrounded conductor colours; it prohibits white, grey, and green. The US pattern is convention and job specification.
necVsCec.conduitBody: Canadian RW90 is unjacketed cross-linked polyethylene. American THHN has a nylon jacket and is thinner for the same copper. RW90 is roughly 14–43% larger in cross-section, depending on size. Canadian EMT is also slightly smaller inside than its US counterpart. The two differences compound.
necVsCec.conduitExample: In one common case, the permitted count differs by a third. We reported nine conductors where the Canadian tables give six.
necVsCec.conduitHeading: 6. Conduit fill: the one that caught us
necVsCec.continuousCecBody: In the Rule 8-104 rated-equipment case, limit the conductor to 80% of its permitted ampacity.
necVsCec.continuousClose: The results land close, but these are not the same operation. Show the operation the local code uses.
necVsCec.continuousHeading: 4. Continuous loads work in opposite directions
necVsCec.coolRoomBody: The NEC lets you increase ampacity below 30°C ambient. The CEC does not. Its single-point rows give no cool-ambient credit below 30°C. Bringing the US habit north silently allows more current than the CEC does.
necVsCec.coolRoomHeading: 3. Canada gives no credit for a cool room
necVsCec.deadCitationBody: Nearly every online source we found cites Canadian colour rules as “Rule 4-038.” In the current 26th edition there is no Rule 4-038. Section 4 ends at Rule 4-036, “Busbar.” The colour rule was Rule 4-038 in the 2012 edition. It is Rule 4-032 now. Sources agreeing with each other is not verification when they are copying each other.
necVsCec.deadCitationHeading: 9. A citation that has been dead for over a decade
necVsCec.deratingBody: At ten current-carrying conductors, the NEC drops to 0.50. The CEC allows 0.70. Same bundle, different answer. This difference is current and easy to miss.
necVsCec.editionBody: Findings checked against CSA C22.1:24, Canadian Electrical Code, Part I, 26th edition (2024), and NEC 2023 (NFPA 70). Adoption is local and local amendments can change the result.
necVsCec.faqAmpacityAnswer: Yes, for the shared sizes and the 60/75/90°C in-raceway columns. The current CEC Tables 2 and 4 match NEC 310.16. Free-air tables still differ.
necVsCec.faqAmpacityQuestion: Are Canadian and US ampacity tables the same?
necVsCec.faqConduitAnswer: No. RW90 is roughly 14–43% larger in cross-section than THHN, and Canadian EMT is slightly smaller inside. T90 lands within about 2% of THHN.
necVsCec.faqConduitQuestion: Is conduit fill the same in Canada and the US?
necVsCec.faqHighLegAnswer: Canada puts the higher-voltage-to-ground conductor on phase A under Rule 4-032. NEC 408.3(E) puts the high leg on phase B.
necVsCec.faqHighLegQuestion: Which phase carries the high leg?
necVsCec.faqVoltageAnswer: The 3% and 5% figures are recommendations in NEC Informational Notes. CEC Rule 8-102 makes voltage drop mandatory in Canada.
necVsCec.faqVoltageQuestion: Is the 3% voltage-drop figure a requirement?
necVsCec.highLegBody: On a 4-wire delta, Canada puts the higher-voltage-to-ground conductor on phase A under Rule 4-032. NEC 408.3(E) puts the high leg on phase B, the centre bus. An electrician looking where their home code taught them finds the wrong conductor.
necVsCec.highLegHeading: 8. The high leg is on a different phase
necVsCec.howWeVerifyLink: Read how VoltDrop checks its numbers.
necVsCec.meterInspectorLine: Confirm the edition in force with the local inspection authority, and use a meter before touching any conductor.
necVsCec.openingBody: We shipped a Canadian conduit-fill calculator that used American conductor dimensions. It gave answers about 50% too permissive. We found it, fixed it, and went looking for what else differs. This is what we found.
necVsCec.subtitle: A verified map of the NEC and Canadian Electrical Code differences that change real answers.
necVsCec.t90Body: T90 nylon, by contrast, lands within about 2% of THHN. It is the Canadian THHN-equivalent. The conductor type matters more than the country.

voltageDrop.increaseTheWireSizeEachAWGStepAnswer: Increase the wire size (each AWG step cuts drop about 21%), raise the system voltage (240 V vs 120 V is a 4x improvement for the same watts), shorten the run, or use a step-up transformer for very long distances.
voltageDrop.inTheNECItLivesInInformationalContinuati: — in the NEC it lives in Informational Notes (3% for a branch circuit, 5% total from service to the farthest load). You generally can't fail a standard inspection on voltage drop alone, with real exceptions: some loads (like fire pumps) have hard drop limits, some local jurisdictions and energy codes adopt stricter enforceable versions, and low-voltage systems often need tighter targets for the reason example 3 shows. Treat 3%/5% as the line between "performs well" and "expect complaints," not as law.

voltageDrop.itSAnOfficialRecommendationInNECAnswer: It's an official recommendation in NEC Informational Notes (3% branch, 5% total), not a generally enforceable requirement — with exceptions like fire pumps, certain energy codes, and local jurisdictions that adopt stricter rules. Treat it as the threshold for good performance.
voltageDrop.itSAnOfficialRecommendationNotAn: it's an official recommendation, not an enforceable requirement
voltageDrop.kBundlesTheWireSResistivityInto: K bundles the wire's resistivity into one field-friendly number. We use the standard conservative values (12.9/21.2); some tools instead use the code's DC resistance table, which is ~20–25% more optimistic. Neither is wrong — conservative leaves margin for temperature and real-world conditions. Every result in our tools opens with "How we calculated this" so you can compare constants against any other source directly.

ohmsLaw.acIsImpedance: On AC it is not. The result is impedance (Z): resistance plus the opposition from anything inductive or capacitive on the circuit, such as a motor winding or ballast. Resistance and impedance are different quantities and are not interchangeable.
ohmsLaw.acTrapHeading: The AC trap — this is the one that matters
ohmsLaw.calculateResistanceAnswer: Divide volts by amps. 120 V at 10 A is 12 Ω on DC. On AC, that same division gives impedance, not resistance.
ohmsLaw.calculateResistanceQuestion: How do I calculate resistance from volts and amps?
ohmsLaw.dcIsResistance: On a DC circuit, volts ÷ amps is resistance. Straightforward.
ohmsLaw.doesntSizeWire: Ohm's law describes a circuit; it does not size a conductor. Wire size depends on ampacity (heat) and voltage drop (distance), neither of which is in this equation. For those, use
ohmsLaw.equations: Know any two and the third follows: V = I × R, I = V ÷ R, R = V ÷ I. Add power and you get P = V × I, P = I² × R, P = V² ÷ R.
ohmsLaw.findWattsAnswer: Use P = I² × R if you know current, or P = V² ÷ R if you know voltage.
ohmsLaw.findWattsQuestion: How do I find watts from ohms?
ohmsLaw.labelsEveryResult: This calculator labels which quantity it is giving you every time. Many Ohm's law calculators simply print “resistance” and move on.
ohmsLaw.ohmsLawTiesThreeQuantities: Ohm's law ties three quantities together:
ohmsLaw.resistanceDefinition: ohms, the resistance to that flow
ohmsLaw.resistivePartExample: The resistive part is roughly R = Z × power factor. A load pulling 10 A at 120 V with a power factor of 0.8 has an impedance of 12 Ω, but a resistive part nearer 9.6 Ω.
ohmsLaw.sameForAcAnswer: The relationship holds, but the ohms are impedance rather than plain resistance. Impedance includes inductive and capacitive opposition, not just resistance. The resistive part is roughly impedance × power factor.
ohmsLaw.sameForAcQuestion: Is Ohm's law the same for AC?
ohmsLaw.sub: V = I × R. Enter any two and get the third, plus the power. And the part most calculators get wrong: on AC, volts ÷ amps is impedance, not resistance.
ohmsLaw.threePhaseAnswer: Because the answer depends on whether the load is wye or delta connected, and this form does not ask. Rather than guess, it declines. Three-phase power calculations work normally.

ohmsLaw.threePhaseRefusal: Ask for ohms on a three-phase circuit and this calculator declines, on purpose. A single resistance figure depends on whether the load is wye or delta connected, and that changes the answer. This form does not ask, and many people wiring a motor do not know off the top of their head. Printing a number anyway would be a guess dressed up as a result.

ohmsLaw.whatIsOhmsLawAnswer: Voltage equals current times resistance: V = I × R. Rearranged, I = V ÷ R and R = V ÷ I. Know any two and you have the third.
ohmsLaw.wireSizeAnswer: No. Wire size comes from ampacity and voltage drop over distance. Ohm's law does not consider either.
ohmsLaw.wireSizeQuestion: Does Ohm's law tell me what size wire to use?
ohmsLaw.workedAc: With the same numbers on single-phase AC at 0.8 power factor: Z = 120 ÷ 10 = 12 Ω, resistive part ≈ 12 × 0.8 = 9.6 Ω, and real power = 120 × 10 × 0.8 = 960 W. Same volts, same amps, different answers — that is the AC trap in one line.
ohmsLaw.workedDc: A 120 V circuit is pulling 10 A on DC. R = V ÷ I = 120 ÷ 10 = 12 Ω, and P = V × I = 1,200 W.

landscape.aDaisyChainRunsOneCableAndTaps: A daisy chain runs one cable and taps each fixture in turn — least cable, biggest difference between first and last. A T split runs one trunk to a dividing point and then two branches in opposite directions, so each branch carries about half the load. A star runs a separate cable from the transformer to every fixture — most cable, best worst-case voltage. A hub runs one trunk out to a junction point and then a short spoke to each fixture. There is no single winner, which is why all four are shown.
landscape.everyOtherCalculatorPutsOneLoadAt: Every other calculator here, including ours, assumes one load at the far end of one run. A landscape run taps fixtures along the cable, so the stretch nearest the transformer carries all of them and the last stretch carries one. The true drop is the sum of the stretches, which is far less than pretending the whole load sits at the end. This tool works it out stretch by stretch.

landscape.hubDistanceHint: How far the trunk runs before it splits. A hub at 0 ft is the same circuit as a star.

landscape.itOverstatesTheDropBecauseItPutsAnswer: It overstates the drop, because it puts the whole load at the far end of the run. In reality the load is spread along the cable, so most of it travels a shorter distance. For fixtures spaced evenly, the ordinary method is too pessimistic by a factor of 2N/(N+1) for N fixtures — about 60% too high for four lights. That pushes you toward heavier cable than the job needs.
landscape.landscapeCableIsAlmostAlwaysCopperHint: Direct-burial landscape cable is almost always copper. 12 AWG is the common choice.
landscape.leaveBlankAndWeAssumeUnityHint: Leave this blank and we assume 1.0, which is a best case — the real current is higher, and so is the real drop.
landscape.mostTransformersHaveSeveralTapsHint: Many transformers offer several taps — 12, 13, 14, 15 V — so you can lift the whole run to make up for the drop.
landscape.noCodeSetsALimitForLowVoltageAnswer: No code sets a mandatory voltage-drop limit for a low-voltage lighting system, and the acceptable window belongs to the fixture manufacturer, not to a rule of thumb. That is why this calculator reports the voltage at each fixture instead of stamping a pass or fail on it. Enter the minimum and maximum from your fixture's data sheet and every tap will be checked against those numbers.
landscape.onADaisyChainTheCableNearestAnswer: On a daisy chain the cable nearest the transformer carries the current of every fixture on the run, while the last stretch carries only one. The drops add up along the way, so each fixture sees a little less voltage than the one before it. Moving to a hub or a star layout, going up a cable size, or lifting the transformer tap all reduce the gap.
landscape.ratedAmpsIsTheMostAccurateHint: Rated amps is the firmest number. Watts is the weakest, because watts alone cannot tell us the current.
landscape.ratedVoltageIsNotTheTapHint: This is what the fixture is designed for, which is not the same as the tap you feed it from. It is what we use to work out the current.
landscape.severalFixturesOnOneCableNotOne: Several fixtures on one cable, not one load at the end. See the voltage at every light, and how four wiring layouts compare.
landscape.theThreeLayoutsInPlainEnglishHeading: The four layouts in plain English
landscape.thereIsNoSingleWinnerAnswer: There is no single winner, which is why this tool shows all four. A daisy chain uses the least cable and gives the widest spread between fixtures. A star gives the highest voltage at the worst fixture but uses the most cable. A T split and a hub both send one trunk out and then divide, so they even the fixtures out — but that shared trunk carries the whole load, which can cost them the worst-case voltage even while it wins on evenness. Compare the numbers for your own run rather than trusting a rule of thumb.
landscape.thisAnswersVoltageDropOnlyItDoesNot: This answers voltage drop only. It does not check that your cable is rated to carry the current, it does not check your transformer's capacity, and it does not evaluate code compliance or your fixture manufacturer's requirements. Use the ampacity check for the current-carrying question, and your fixture's data sheet for the voltage window.

landscape.twoFixturesAtTheSameDistanceHint: Two fixtures at the same distance are treated as two lights on one tap. Rows can go in any order.
landscape.weDoNotInventAVoltageLimitHint: We do not invent a voltage limit. Enter the window from your fixture's data sheet and every tap gets checked against it.

solar.becauseLowVoltageMeansHugeCurrentAnswer: Because low voltage means enormous current, and a tight percentage of a small voltage is a tiny number of volts. A 3000 W inverter on a 12 V bank draws around 250 A at nominal voltage and more as the bank sags. Meanwhile 1% of 12 V is 0.12 V — that is the entire budget for the whole out-and-back trip. Short cables and high system voltage are the two things that help most, which is why larger installations use 24 or 48 V.
solar.becauseTheLossIsContinuousAnswer: The 3% figure is a house-wiring convention, where the load runs occasionally. A panel circuit loses that voltage every hour the sun is up, for the life of the system, so the same percentage costs far more. On a battery-to-inverter cable it is worse than a cost: the inverter sees battery voltage minus the cable drop, so a sagging cable can trip its low-voltage cutout while the bank still holds usable charge. That is why the pre-filled targets here are tighter — though they are starting points you should set yourself, not requirements.
solar.doesThisSizeMyFusesQuestion: Does this size my fuses or breakers?
solar.eachOfTheThreeCircuitsTakesItsCurrent: Each of the three circuits takes its current from a different place, and using the wrong one is the easiest way to get a badly wrong answer. Panels are closer to a current source, so their operating current barely moves. A charge controller is rated by what it can put out, which is not what the panels put in. And an inverter's draw climbs as the battery falls, so dividing watts by the nominal bank voltage understates it exactly when the cable can least afford it.
solar.itDependsOnTheCircuitAnswer: It depends on the circuit, which is why this tool asks differently for each one. For a panel circuit use the array's operating current, Imp, from the data sheet — not the short-circuit figure. For a charge controller to a battery, use the controller's maximum output current, not the panel rating. For a battery to an inverter, use the maximum continuous DC input current — and if you work it out from watts, divide by the lowest battery voltage you will allow rather than the nominal 12 or 24 V, because the current rises as the bank sags.
solar.measureOneWayWeDoubleItHint: Measure the distance one way only. We double it, because the current goes out and comes back.
solar.noItAnswersVoltageDropOnlyAnswer: No. This answers voltage drop only. It does not size overcurrent protection, it does not check that the conductor can carry the current, it applies no temperature correction, and it applies no PV sizing factors. Battery systems in particular can deliver extremely high fault current, so the protection and disconnect arrangements need to follow the battery and equipment manufacturer's instructions. Check the ampacity separately and use whichever size is larger.
solar.nominalVoltageUnderstatesTheCurrentHint: We divide by the LOWEST battery voltage, not the nominal 12 or 24 V. The inverter still has to deliver its full output when the bank has sagged, so that is when the current — and the drop — is worst.
solar.onABranchCircuitAN3%DropIs: On a branch circuit a 3% drop is a rule of thumb for a load that runs now and then. Solar changes both halves of that. The loss is continuous, so it compounds into real lost energy, and the voltages are low, so a small percentage is a very small number of volts to spend. 1% of 12 V is 0.12 V for the entire out-and-back trip.
solar.scenarioBatteryWhy: The tightest one. Drop here costs power and cutout margin.
solar.scenarioControllerWhy: Drop here makes the controller misread the battery.
solar.scenarioPvWhy: Drop here is lost yield, every hour the sun is up.
solar.solarCircuitsAreTighterThanHouseWiring: Solar circuits are tighter than house wiring, and each one takes its current from a different place. Pick the circuit and we ask for the right number.
solar.thisAnswersVoltageDropOnlyAndNothingElse: This answers voltage drop and nothing else. It does not evaluate ampacity, temperature, overcurrent protection, disconnects, grounding, or code compliance, and it does not handle an inverter's AC output — use the voltage drop calculator for that, which knows about single- and three-phase. Treat the size here as one of two answers you need, and use whichever is larger.

solarWireSize.biggerWireAnswer: Because the voltage is low. The same watts at 12 V draw twenty times the current they would at 240 V, and voltage drop scales with current.

solarWireSize.inverterRunQuestion: Does this size the wire from my battery to my inverter?
solarWireSize.lostYieldBody: Every volt dropped in the wire is a volt that never reaches the controller. On a battery system it also eats the margin before the low-voltage cutout trips.
solarWireSize.lostYieldHeading: 2. Array voltage drop is lost yield
solarWireSize.lowVoltageBody: 3% of 240 V is 7.2 V — plenty of room. 3% of 12 V is 0.36 V. There is no headroom at low voltage, which is why solar practice runs tighter than the branch-circuit convention: roughly 2% on panel circuits, tighter still between battery and inverter.

solarWireSize.otherDcRuns: For controller-to-battery, size on the controller's maximum output, not its input. For battery-to-inverter, size on maximum continuous DC input at the low-voltage cutout. solarWireSize.outOfRangeBody: If the result is out of range, the tool says so explicitly rather than handing back the largest conductor it happens to know about.
solarWireSize.panelCoverage: This page is about the panel-to-controller run.
solarWireSize.rightCurrentBody: For the panel-to-controller run, the current that matters is the array's Imp at Vmp — the current at the maximum power point — not the short-circuit rating and not a figure worked back from the panel's watt rating at nominal voltage. Nominal understates it.
solarWireSize.rightCurrentHeading: Use the right current, not the nameplate
solarWireSize.shortCircuitAnswer: Not for voltage drop. Use the current at maximum power (Imp), which is what the array actually delivers in operation. Short-circuit current has its own uses in overcurrent sizing.
solarWireSize.shortCircuitQuestion: Should I use the panel's short-circuit current?
solarWireSize.sub: Wire size for a solar array, where the usual 3% rule of thumb quietly stops working. Panel current is not the number on the label, and 3% of 12 volts is a third of a volt.
solarWireSize.targetsBody: The drop targets this tool uses are starting points from common solar practice, not code requirements. There is no code rule that says 2%. Your equipment manufacturer may specify something tighter, and their number wins. The tool shows the target it used so you can change it knowingly rather than inherit it silently.
